That's why the decision stays with me.

articles.author: Nathan C.
articles.description:
Line 60 of my model's prompt says "Never output em-dashes, in any form." Line 976 says it again, in case it forgot. The agent it runs in says it a third time. It still slips them in, so that agent ends up ripping them out of every reply in code, a token at a time, as it streams.
That's when I admitted the prompt had gotten out of hand.
Every version of Onyx, the model behind my local AI agent Flash, has secretly been a prompt. Not fine-tuned weights. A Modelfile wrapped around an open-weights base, with the system prompt doing all the work. Every time Onyx did something dumb, I wrote a rule. Onyx 2.6's prompt is now 174,826 characters long. That's about 980 lines of rules the model has to keep in mind while it works, and every new chat pays for all of them before it writes its first word. …
articles.title: I'm finally fine-tuning my model, because its prompt hit 175,000 characters

articles.description:
The Big Picture: From Text to Natural‑Sounding Voice


If you’ve ever wondered how a string of characters magically becomes a human‑like utterance, you’re not alone. Modern neural text‑to‑speech (TTS) systems have come a long way from the robotic “speak” of the 90s. Under the hood they combine three big ideas:
Acoustic modeling – a deep network predicts a spectrogram (a visual representation of sound frequencies) from raw text.


Vocoder synthesis – another network turns that spectrogram into an audio waveform.


Speaker conditioning – a set of vectors (often called “embeddings”) tells the model who should speak, enabling voice cloning and style control.
Together these components produce speech that can convey emotion, prosody, and even a speaker’s unique timbre. Let’s unpack each piece an…
articles.title: How Neural Text-to-Speech Actually Works

articles.author: Charan Reddy Rachumalla
articles.description:
Every Kafka consumer application calls poll(). Very few developers can list what happens inside it.
That gap shows up at the worst time: a consumer that hangs, a group that rebalances in a loop, a commit that keeps failing. Each of those failures lives in a specific step of the flow below. The flow is seven steps. The first is setup, the next four are a handshake, and the last two are the steady state the consumer spends its life in.
Application code builds a KafkaConsumer with bootstrap.servers and a group.id, then calls subscribe() with the topic list.
subscribe() only registers interest. Nothing is fetched, nothing is assigned, no broker knows the consumer exists yet. Every step that follows is driven by poll() — it is the engine of the entire client, and the handshake below unfolds acr…
articles.title: Every Step Runs Inside poll(): The Kafka Consumer Flow, End to End

articles.author: Katana Works
articles.description:
If you’re building a multi-level game in GDevelop, you do not need a separate scene for every stage. There’s a pattern using global variables and external layouts that keeps your entire game running on a single reusable scene.

Here’s how it works at a high level.
One global variable drives everything. Create a number variable called current_level in your project’s global variables. Initialize it to 1. This is your level pointer.
External layouts hold level geometry. Instead of new scenes, you create external layouts named with a consistent pattern — Level1, Level2, Level3, etc. Each layout uses your main game scene as its base, so it has access to all existing objects.
Dynamic loading at scene start. In your main scene’s event sheet, add a “Beginning of scene” event with the action “Create objects from external layout.” The layout name is an expression:
"Level" + GlobalVariableString(current_level)
Set X, Y, Z origin to 0. Add a Trigger Once condition so it doesn’t fire every frame.
Level transitions. When the player collides with a door and presses the interact key, increment current_level by 1 and change to the same scene. The scene reloads, the beginning-of-scene event fires, and the next layout gets pulled in automatically.
Don’t forget camera boundaries. If your levels are different sizes, you need per-level camera boundary logic. Check the value of current_level and set boundaries accordingly, or your camera will float off into empty space.
This pattern scales well — I’ve used it on projects with 20+ levels and the project file stays manageable. No duplicated event sheets, no object sprawl across scenes.
I made a video walkthrough that covers the full implementation if you prefer to see it built step by step:
https://youtu.be/KBtNvKsRlwk
articles.title: Dynamic Multi-Level Loading in GDevelop (Without Duplicating Scenes)

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a news monitoring service that detects semantically near-duplicate stories, the evaluation set is the product requirement: it tells you if a result is relevant, attributable, and safe to show to a reviewer.
The tempting implementation is one giant vector collection and a generous top-k. It looks quick in a demo, then quietly mixes tenants, editions, and wire copies. A grounded system makes each decision visible. I care about that audit trail more than a clever similarity score.
Start with the answer a user will see, then map it to a retrieval contract. A contract for “find duplicates of this alert” should name the tenant, time window, source scope, language, and the evi…
